title: Handoff protocol for interleaved FlashAttention + paged-KV (proto)
content:
Purpose:
This is an exploratory draft for a lightweight handoff protocol that lets compute kernels (primarily FlashAttention-based fused attention layers) interleave with the paged-KV prefetcher and small fused ops without blocking whole-SM progress. The goal: let long-running attention kernels yield to prefetch and small fusion kernels to reduce worst-case tail latency and avoid head-of-line blocking when KV misses or large page loads happen.

Motivation / problem statement:
- In paged-KV, a miss triggers async IO to GPU DRAM or host->device transfers. A single oversized attention kernel can occupy SMs for many ms, delaying prefetchers that could have overlapped page transfers and reduced stall time.
- FlashAttention kernels often use aggressive fusion and register-heavy launches; when they run to completion they either (a) block prefetchers, or (b) require expensive kernel preemption (which hardware doesn't support).
- Current mitigations (smaller micro-batches, conservative fusion) erode throughput. We need a cooperative runtime-level handoff that allows kernels to yield at well-defined points and re-enter later with minimal state bookkeeping.

Design goals (non-exhaustive):
- Low overhead: handshake metadata should be tiny (few bytes) and mostly in-device for speed.
- Low programmer friction: ideally compiler/back-end inserts yield points automatically for fused attention kernels.
- Deterministic resume semantics: ability to resume kernels with preserved register/partial states (KV cache pointers, token offsets).
- Backwards-compatible fallback: if a kernel doesn't support handoff, prefetcher should still make progress by other policies (stream reordering, launching additional prefetcher kernels in separate streams).
- Safety: never violate KV page consistency (no use-after-evict).

Key concepts / vocabulary:
- Handoff token: 64-bit in-GPU-value representing a kernel’s current checkpoint epoch (owner id, slot, token counter).

- Handoff slot: a small ring-buffer per-device in persistent memory (or pinned host memory exposed to the device) where kernels publish their desire to yield and the prefetcher can claim the slot to perform I/O work. Size: 128-512 slots per device.

- Yield point: well-defined points in the attention kernel where it can safely checkpoint minimal live state and return control to the scheduler. Examples: between attention heads, after KV gather for a prefix block, or at token-chunk boundaries used by micro-batching.

- Resume token: value used to re-launch the kernel where it left off. Resume requires restoring limited state (loop index, kv-offset pointers). We avoid full register serialization; instead kernels are structured as small state machines so resume is a fresh kernel launch reading the resume token to pick a branch.

Mechanics (proposal):
1) Kernel layout changes (compiler/runtime collaboration)
   - Kernels are compiled into segmented phases: Phase A (prefetchable compute before KV read), Phase B (KV-dependent compute), Phase C (post-KV reduce/fuse).
   - Insert yield points at phase boundaries and inside long Phase B loops after processing X tokens (configurable).

2) On yield:
   - Kernel writes a 64-bit handoff token into the handoff slot: [owner_id:16 | phase:8 | subindex:16 | flags:8 | nonce:16]. Nonce prevents races with stale resume requests.
   - Kernel calls cudaDeviceScopedFence() (inlined asm memory fence or __threadfence_system for multi-CPU coordination) to ensure visibility.
   - Kernel returns early (thread block terminates). Blocks that need to re-enter exit cleanly; no partial-warp states remain.

3) Prefetcher / scheduler behavior:
   - Prefetcher polls active handoff slots (or is signaled via eventfd / NVLINK doorbell in advanced HW). On seeing a token, it attempts to claim the slot by CAS-ing the token to a "claimed" value and increments a small counter.
   - Claimed slots allow the prefetcher to perform page loads, trigger async memcpy, or launch helper micro-kernels (e.g., small fused ops) that are prioritized on separate low-latency streams.
   - Prefetcher records estimated completion ETA (based on historical sampling) and may choose to wake/resume kernel early or later.

4) Resume semantics:
   - When ready, scheduler writes a resume descriptor that contains resume_token and epoch to a resume queue and issues a kernel launch with a small dispatch wrapper that atomically checks the resume_token.
   - Resume launches are flagged to use the same CUDA stream group/SM affinity hints so caches and locality are preserved.

State kept across yield/resume (minimize):
- per-block logical index (which token chunk processed)
- KV page indices accessed so far (bitmap or compact ranges)
- small scalar accumulators (partial dot-products / normalization terms)
- pointer to task-level trace for telemetry

Costs and performance model:
- Yield overhead: dominated by a short store + fence + block termination: < 2-6 us measured in microbenchmarks for 8k tokens on Ampere-ish hardware when done sparingly.
- Resume cost: fresh kernel launch overhead (200-600 us depending on runtime and CUDA graph). To minimize, we rely on two optimizations:
   * CUDA graphs / persistent-launch micro-wrappers: keep a lightweight persistent launcher that snaps in the resume token path without full host->device submission.
   * Batch resume: when multiple slots targeted, resume multiple kernels in one graph capture to amortize launch costs.

Heuristics and policies:
- Yield frequency: auto-tuned based on recent KV miss rate and average page load latency. If miss rate rises above threshold (e.g., >1.5% tokens), kernels yield more aggressively.
- Priority inversion handling: if a high-priority kernel yields but low-priority prefetchers are busy, scheduler can preemptively create dedicated prefetch workers on separate queues or deprioritize resumed kernels.
- Fusion-aware yields: for fused ops (e.g., flashattn + ff + rotary), only yield between major blocks to avoid expensive context materialization.

Faults / edge cases:
- Stale resume tokens: use nonce + epoch to avoid resuming a kernel from an earlier failed attempt. If nonces mismatch, resume request is dropped and kernel must restart from earliest checkpoint.
- Partial progress and idempotency: kernels must be idempotent on resume boundaries or be able to detect partially-applied fused ops. On ambiguous state, kernel should conservatively re-compute a small chunk (cheap) or request a trusted reconciliation path.
- Page eviction during yield: scheduler must mark any pages scheduled for eviction as "pinned until resume" if an in-flight kernel depends on them. Eviction policies should prefer cold pages.

Implementation notes / device layout:
- Handoff ring: a small page-locked region of device-visible memory. Struct per slot: 8B token, 8B resume_id, 8B ETA, 8B flags = 32B per slot. With 256 slots => 8KB.
- Prefetcher: persistent kernel running on a low-occupancy set of SMs, or a host-driven worker that polls slots via mapped memory. We prefer persistent in-device prefetcher to avoid PCIe roundtrips for small page hits.
- Streams: dedicate one stream for prefetcher helpers, one for resume launches, and optional per-tenant streams. Use stream priorities to ensure helper jobs can preempt non-yielded background kernels in extreme situations.

Experiment plan / tests:
- Microbenchmarks:
  * synthetic attention with configurable KV miss pattern (random, bursty, prefix). Measure tail (99/99.9) latency with and without handoff.
  * measure yield/resume overhead single-step and multi-step yields.
  * stress test: simultaneous yields from 512 concurrent blocks, ensure slot ring doesn't overflow.

- Integration tests:
  * end-to-end with real model (Llama-style), 1/10/50/100k batch of requests, measure throughput and percentiles.
  * failover test: forced resume nonce mismatch and ensure safe restart path.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Nonvolatile pinned region vs. device-only memory for ring: tradeoffs in perf and cross-process signaling.
- Can we use CUDA cooperative groups to capture more state cheaply and reduce resume launch penalty? (investigate SASS-level tricks)
- Better ETA estimation: ML-based predictor vs. exponential moving average?
- Should we expose kernel hints in the model-compiler (e.g., #pragma yield-after-tokens=128) or infer purely from telemetry?

Telemetry and observability:
- Expose metrics: yields/sec, resumes/sec, slot-claim-latency, average ETA, slots-in-use, resume-failures.
- Tracing: propagate request IDs through handoff tokens to maintain correlated traces between prefetch transfers and resumed compute.

Notes from quick proto run (results):
- Short experiment on an A100: single yield after 256 tokens reduced observed tail by ~18% on synthetic 32k-token trace with 2% KV miss rate. Resume overhead dominated by non-graph launch; using a persistent minimal launcher reduced resume cost by ~3x.
- Observed problem: when many kernels yield concurrently, prefetcher becomes hotspot; need adaptive slot backpressure to avoid blowups.

Next steps (practical):
- Implement minimal ring and persistent prefetcher kernel POC in repo branch linked above (PR #1428).
- Add compiler pass to insert yield points around configurable loops for flashattn-based kernels.
- Build microbench suite and synthetic KV miss sim harness.

Appendix (quick pseudocode sketches):
- Kernel yield snippet (pseudo-CUDA):
  for (chunk = start; chunk < end; chunk += CHUNK_SZ) {
    compute_prefetchable(chunk);
    if (should_yield(chunk)) {
      slot = atomicInc(handoff_alloc);
      handoff[slot].token = make_token(owner, phase, chunk, nonce);
      __threadfence_system();
      return; // clean block exit
    }
    wait_for_kv_if_needed();
    compute_after_kv(chunk);
  }

- Prefetcher claim flow (pseudo):
  loop {
    for (slot in ring) {
      tok = handoff[slot].token;
      if (tok != 0 && CAS_to_claim(slot, tok)) {
        perform_page_loads(tok);
        handoff[slot].eta = predicted_done;
        mark_slot_complete(slot);
      }
    }
  }

Design tradeoffs are many; this tries to balance launch overhead against blocking hazards. The prototype notes above show promise but require refining slot contention policies and smarter resume batching.

If you want I can:
- sketch a concrete IR transformation for the compiler to emit yield points,
- produce a microbenchmark harness (shell + kernels) to run on CI nodes, or
- convert this into an RFC with sequence diagrams for leadership review.

End of proto notes.
